revision.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
revision.summary:
Security Alliance (SEAL) proposes expanding its existing intelligence program into an automated threat intelligence and response capability for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The initiative will strengthen the collection, normalization, enrichment, correlation, and distribution of intelligence gathered through real-world incidents, security research, and ecosystem partnerships.

By combining automation with expert human analysis, SEAL Intel will deliver verified indicators of compromise, actionable threat alerts, machine-readable intelligence feeds, and tailored defensive recommendations. The goal is to help Ethereum organizations identify emerging threats earlier, understand how attackers operate, and take preventive action before similar attacks spread across the ecosystem.

The initiative will also strengthen SEAL's Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) capabilities, enabling trusted participants to exchange intelligence, coordinate responses, and improve their collective security posture.

sections.why:
Ethereum security threats increasingly extend beyond smart contract vulnerabilities to the infrastructure, developers, employees, and operational systems supporting blockchain organizations. Social engineering, malware, compromised developer environments, supply-chain attacks, and increasingly sophisticated AI-assisted campaigns require security teams to identify and respond to threats quickly. Yet relevant intelligence remains fragmented across incident reports, malicious-domain lists, security vendors, on-chain monitoring, private reporting channels, and external research. Traditional security intelligence providers often lack the Web3-specific context needed to connect these signals to real-world blockchain threats, while the cost of enterprise intelligence services can limit access for smaller organizations.

SEAL Intel aims to close this gap by transforming intelligence gathered through real incidents into verified, actionable information that Ethereum organizations can use to protect themselves. By automating collection, enrichment, correlation, and distribution while preserving expert analyst review, SEAL will deliver timely alerts, machine-readable feeds, and tailored defensive recommendations. Rather than simply receiving isolated indicators or retrospective reports, participating organizations will be able to understand how emerging threats operate, determine whether their infrastructure is exposed, and take preventive action. The initiative will also strengthen coordination and two-way intelligence sharing across SEAL's existing ecosystem network.
sections.in_scope:
The initiative will expand SEAL Intel's existing capabilities into a more automated, scalable, and coordinated threat intelligence service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. Grant funding will support intelligence collection and normalization, automated processing and correlation, analyst workflows, actionable intelligence delivery, ISAC coordination, and independently verifiable partner adoption.

**1. Intelligence Collection and Normalization**

Ethereum threat intelligence is fragmented across sources, formats, and threat categories. SEAL will address these challenges through:

**Source aggregation:** Automated connectors will collect relevant intelligence from a curated set of open-source feeds, security firms, on-chain monitoring systems, vulnerability disclosures, social channels, private reporting groups, and partner ISACs/CERTs. Sources will be reviewed for reliability, relevance, and sharing permissions.

**Data normalization:** Intelligence arriving as free-text reports, chat messages, spreadsheets, and incompatible feed formats will be normalized using STIX 2.1, with documented conventions for Ethereum-specific indicators including wallet addresses, smart contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains. Automated extraction will transform supported unstructured reports into records suitable for further analysis.

**Threat classification:** Intelligence will be categorized across smart contract exploits, phishing and wallet-draining campaigns, malware, social engineering, infrastructure and supply-chain compromises, and state-linked threat actor activity. Classification by threat category and affected participant type will help identify coverage gaps and improve relevance filtering.

**2. Automated Processing, Enrichment, and Correlation**

The initiative will automate repeatable intelligence-processing tasks while retaining human-in-the-loop review before intelligence is released through the proposed analyst-approved workflows.

Processing will include:

- **Correctness:** Validate indicators and intelligence claims, assess source reliability, and assign confidence levels to reduce false positives.
- **Enrichment:** Connect indicators to relevant malware, infrastructure, incidents, campaigns, and threat actors where supported by evidence.
- **Correlation:** Identify relationships between newly ingested intelligence, existing SEAL records, and observations collected through incident-response and reporting channels.
- **Relevance:** Determine which participant types are affected, the urgency of the threat, and the defensive actions organizations should consider.

The resulting intelligence records will combine structured indicators with supporting context explaining how threats operate, their potential impact, and relevant defensive measures.

**3. Actionable Intelligence and Recommendations**

SEAL will expand beyond primarily informative intelligence reporting to provide more actionable outputs derived from observed attacker behavior and real-world incidents.

Analyst-approved recommendations will be tailored to relevant participant profiles, including DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, wallet providers, infrastructure operators, security firms, government organizations, and institutional participants.

Recommendations may include investigating malicious infrastructure, blocking suspicious domains, reviewing authentication controls, rotating compromised credentials, examining software dependencies, or implementing additional monitoring.

The objective is to help organizations understand not only what threat indicators exist, but also how the underlying attack operates and what they can do to reduce exposure.

**4. Intelligence Distribution and Alerting**

SEAL will develop tiered intelligence products matched to urgency and audience:

- **Flash alerts:** Timely notifications concerning active or emerging threats.
- **Tailored defensive recommendations:** Actionable guidance relevant to specific organization types and infrastructure.
- **Periodic intelligence reports:** Research covering significant campaigns, attacker trends, emerging techniques, and defensive recommendations.
- **Machine-readable intelligence feeds:** Authenticated REST API and TAXII 2.1 endpoints allowing organizations to integrate intelligence into existing security tooling.

These outputs will draw from consistent, validated intelligence records to improve accuracy and relevance across reporting and distribution channels.

**5. ISAC Participation and Two-Way Intelligence Sharing**

The initiative will strengthen SEAL's Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) by supporting both intelligence distribution and participant contributions.

Planned capabilities include:

- **Intelligence submission:** Approved channels for participants to submit incidents, indicators, and observations through secure messaging, APIs, or other supported interfaces.
- **Protected sharing:** Appropriate anonymization, redaction, contributor permissions, and TLP 2.0 markings to protect sensitive information.
- **Requests for information:** Mechanisms for participants to request context or determine whether others are observing similar threats.
- **Incident coordination:** Facilitation of information sharing and coordinated responses when threats affect multiple organizations.
- **Community collaboration:** Trusted working groups and liaison with other ISACs, CERTs, and security organizations.
- **Contributor feedback:** Information about how submitted intelligence was processed and whether it contributed to released intelligence.

**6. Trust, Security, and Governance**

The expanded intelligence service will incorporate vetted participation, role-based access, source attribution, TLP 2.0 information handling, redaction, access and sharing audit logs, and processes for identifying false positives or stale indicators.

Appropriate safeguards will address unauthorized access, malicious submissions, intelligence corrections, and restricted redistribution.

**7. Partner Pilot and Performance Measurement**

SEAL will conduct phased integrations with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations to evaluate the operational usefulness of its feeds, alerts, and recommendations.

Performance will be measured through:

- **Participation:** Active organizations, integrations, and intelligence contributions.
- **Speed:** Time from detection to validation and dissemination.
- **Usage:** Feed/API consumption and documented defensive actions.
- **Quality:** False-positive rates, relevance, and participant feedback.

The six-month delivery plan will cover initial ingestion and normalization, operational analyst workflows and alerting, and a partner adoption pilot. The specific acceptance criteria and funding allocations are detailed in the milestones.

**Grant-Funded Resources**

The proposed $267,000 budget supports engineering, intelligence analysis, partner integrations, delivery management, infrastructure, and independent technical verification. The current planning model allocates $108,000 to engineering, $54,000 to intelligence analysis, $60,000 to partner integration, $15,000 to delivery management, $18,000 to infrastructure, and $12,000 to independent review. These allocations remain subject to validation against actual staffing commitments and project costs.
sections.out_scope:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom investigations, security assessments, or consulting engagements.
- Automated modification of participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, or phishing-takedown platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted intelligence without appropriate authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the agreed grant scope and milestones.

The initiative expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.
sections.team:
Security Alliance (SEAL) will deliver this initiative through its established threat intelligence program, drawing on experienced security researchers, engineers, and incident-response specialists across its existing operations.

Oskar (@blackbigswan) — SEAL Intel Lead: Leads SEAL's threat intelligence initiative, overseeing intelligence priorities, technical direction, analyst workflows, research coordination, and the development of actionable intelligence capabilities for Ethereum ecosystem participants.

Joe Dobson — Security Research and Threat Intelligence: Formerly of Mandiant, Joe contributes expertise in cybersecurity research, malware analysis, and the development of actionable threat intelligence products and workflows tailored to enterprise and government security organizations.

Peter Kacherginsky — Security Research and Intelligence Contributor: Peter brings extensive cybersecurity expertise spanning traditional security and Web3. He operates BlockThreat, a recognized security research publication, and contributes specialized research and intelligence expertise on a limited part-time basis. Relevant BlockThreat on-chain intelligence is expected to become available through SEAL Intel, subject to applicable data-sharing permissions.

Matta (@mattaereal) — Security Frameworks and Technical Research: Matta leads SEAL Security Frameworks and is the founder of The Red Guild. His work focuses on translating practical security knowledge into structured guidance for blockchain organizations. He will contribute expertise in security frameworks, threat modeling, and mapping intelligence gathered from real-world incidents into actionable defensive recommendations, helping connect SEAL Intel's research with broader security practices across the Ethereum ecosystem.

Dickson Wu — On-Chain Security and Incident Response: Dickson contributes to SEAL Safe Harbor, an initiative supporting the secure recovery of digital assets during critical protocol incidents. His experience in on-chain security, protocol operations, and incident coordination will help inform the analysis of blockchain-specific threats and the development of practical recommendations for protocols and other ecosystem participants.

Additional SEAL Contributors: SEAL's existing engineering, intelligence, and incident-response personnel will support data integrations, automation, API development, intelligence distribution, and partner onboarding. Specific engineering assignments and time commitments will be finalized with the delivery team.

Funding and relationships: The initiative has a proposed total budget of $267,000, comprising $200,000 sought from TheDAO and $67,000 in prospective external support from the Ethereum Foundation, which is not yet committed. SEAL maintains established relationships across the Ethereum ecosystem and operates existing intelligence, incident-response, and security research infrastructure.
sections.why_grant:
SEAL Intel expands an established operational threat intelligence program rather than building a new organization or platform from scratch. Security Alliance already operates incident-response and intelligence-reporting infrastructure, conducts extensive malware and threat actor research, maintains OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities, and distributes security information throughout the Ethereum ecosystem.

**Existing capabilities include:**

- **100+ ecosystem communication channels and hotlines** connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain participants. These channels support incident coordination, threat reporting, and timely intelligence sharing.
- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake** through `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting initial incident response, on-chain tracing, security reporting, and industry coordination.
- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately **5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly** and contributes to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's `eth-phishing-detect` enables identified malicious frontends to be blocked within minutes of detection.
- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain threats. Outputs include indicators of compromise (IOCs), tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), campaign research, malicious-domain takedown coordination, and EV code-signing certificate revocation efforts.
- **Public research and intelligence reporting:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and weekly operational statistics through SEAL Radar and other public channels.
- **Existing intelligence workflows:** SEAL maintains research processes and OpenCTI-related capabilities for collecting, organizing, and analyzing intelligence.

**Why grant funding provides leverage:** The proposed work builds on existing researchers, operational infrastructure, incident visibility, intelligence sources, and ecosystem relationships. Funding will support the incremental engineering and operational effort needed to automate collection, normalization, enrichment, correlation, and distribution rather than finance the creation of a new intelligence organization from scratch. Existing work and previously funded deliverables will be distinguished from grant-funded additions.

**Public evidence:**

- SEAL research and reporting: https://radar.securityalliance.org/
- SEAL GitHub: https://github.com/security-alliance
- Lazarus Group research: https://lazarus.group/
- Public intelligence dataset: https://github.com/security-alliance/lazarus-group-data
- Binance incident research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/tradertraitor-vs-contagious-interview-a-look-at-binances-initial-incident-report/
- DPRK malware research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/vs-code-tasks-abuse-by-contagious-interview-dprk/
- Weekly operational statistics: https://radar.securityalliance.org/seal-weekly-stats-20-27-oct-2026/
sections.commitments:
SEAL will deliver the agreed grant-funded capabilities and provide independently verifiable evidence against the milestones, including documented integrations, intelligence-processing workflows, distribution mechanisms, and operational adoption.

SEAL intends to maintain the capabilities developed through this initiative as part of its existing intelligence operations after the six-month grant period. Long-term sustainability will be supported through continued ecosystem funding and a proposed enhanced Intel/ISAC donor package, currently envisioned at approximately $50,000 per participating organization annually. This donor model is prospective and does not represent committed revenue.

Grant-funded public-good outputs will be distinguished from additional donor-supported services. Sensitive intelligence will remain subject to contributor permissions, confidentiality requirements, and applicable TLP restrictions.

**Licensing and source availability:** SEAL will specify the licenses and publication commitments applicable to grant-funded software, documentation, schemas, and other deliverables in the final agreement. Restricted intelligence and confidential source material will not be publicly released where doing so would violate applicable permissions.

**Maintenance:** Named maintainers, the minimum post-grant support period, and the operating budget required to sustain the funded capabilities will be confirmed before the grant agreement is finalized.

**Measurable targets:** The initiative will be evaluated against the agreed quantitative milestones for source integrations, normalization, extraction accuracy, analyst productivity, alert delivery, intelligence distribution, and independent partner adoption.

Any exceptions concerning public release of sensitive intelligence, source-code availability, or other standard grant requirements will be expressly disclosed and agreed before implementation.

milestones.name: Data ingestion and normalization
criteria: Automated connectors/data feeds run in production for at least 10 sources across at least 5 source classes, and the source list is provided to the reviewer.
100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators (addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, dApp domains).
On a test set of 50 unstructured reports, automated extraction recovers at least 90% of the indicators an analyst identifies by hand.
At least 50% of observables ingested over a 14-day period are linked to an entity (threat actor, campaign, malware family, or incident), not stored as standalone observables.
An automated overlap report runs at least daily for 14 consecutive days, flagging matches between newly ingested external intelligence and SEAL’s privately gathered data.

milestones.name: Correlation, analyst workflows and alert delivery
criteria: Median analyst time to produce a report through the new workflow is at least 50% lower than a manual baseline, measured on 10 reports against 5 baseline reports timed at the start of the grant.
Over a 30-day period, every alert for a relevant threat reaches participants within 24 hours of detection, and the median time is reported.
At least 2 intelligence reports per month with recommendations are produced through the new workflow and distributed. (Volume may vary depending on incidents unfolding)
A TAXII 2.1 and REST endpoint is live with authentication, and an external test client can pull records filtered by threat category, participant type, and TLP level.
Recommendation templates exist for different participant profiles (protocol, infrastructure provider, wallet, exchange, security firm, government, institution etc.), with one issued example of each.
The partner onboarding guide, API reference, and TLP handling policy are published.

milestones.name: Partner adoption pilot (adoption)
criteria: 6 independent organizations, covering at least 3 participant types, each pulled from the feed or API on at least 20 days of a 30-day window, shown by access logs.
At least 4 of those organizations confirm in writing that the TAXII or REST feed is integrated into their own security tooling.
At least 4 of those organizations each submitted a contribution that became a released record.
At least 3 organizations each confirm in writing a specific action (a block, credential rotation, patch, or takedown) taken because of an alert or recommendation
At least 6 further organizations are onboarded and pulling from the feed after the pilot cohort, with at least 2 joining in each of the final two months.
